days.title: The Beginning of the End
days.summary: The resurrection of Lazarus was Jesus' last great public miracle — and, at the same time, the spark that sealed the religious leaders' decision to kill Him.
body: The resurrection of Lazarus was the last great miracle Jesus performed during His public ministry. At the same time, it became the turning point for the religious leaders, setting off the sequence of events that would mark the final scenes of Christ's life. Even knowing what was to come, Jesus performed this miracle anyway — the awareness of the approaching pain and loss likely explains the intensity of the emotions present in the account.

The priests' hatred intensified with the resurrection, even in broad daylight before a crowd of witnesses. No trick could explain that display — and precisely because of that, the enmity against Him became even more relentless.

Jesus knew that time was running out, and repeatedly sought to prepare the disciples, revealing what was to come (John 12:7,8,23,24,27,31,32). Christ moved forward toward death, driven by a love more intense than the suffering that awaited Him — abandoning humanity would have caused Him greater anguish than the cross itself.

What does it mean to say that Jesus' love was 'greater than the suffering' that awaited Him?
How did the nearness of pain not stop Jesus from acting with compassion?

days.title: Two Reactions, Same Mistake
days.summary: Religious leaders and crowds reacted in opposite ways to the resurrection of Lazarus — one group wanted to destroy Jesus, the other to crown Him — but both, deep down, were mistaken about who He really was.
body: After the resurrection of Lazarus, we see two very different reactions: one from the religious leaders, another from the crowds that followed Jesus. The leaders gathered because they were alarmed at the influence they had been losing (John 11:45-48). Caiaphas tried to reassure them, insisting there was an obvious way out: "Let's kill Him, and the problem is over."

The other reaction came from the people. When Jesus arrived in Jerusalem, He was received amid celebration — His triumphal entry drew even more attention, amid shouts of "Hosanna!" (John 12:13). Many believed they were witnessing the arrival of a new King — which was also true, but not in the way they expected.

These two groups interpreted Jesus' life in very different ways: one wanted to destroy Him, the other to crown Him. Deep down, however, both were driven by self-interest, because no one stopped to listen to what Jesus was really saying about His mission.
reflect: Are you surprised to see religious leaders, who knew the Bible, planning Jesus' death? What warning does this bring?
How can we listen to what Jesus really says, instead of shaping His image to fit our own interests?
In what areas have you already 'twisted' who Jesus is to fit your own expectations?

days.title: Someone Was Listening
days.summary: While Judas and Simon criticized Mary's gesture as wasteful, John reveals that she was, in fact, the only person who was truly paying attention to what Jesus was saying.
body: After the resurrection of Lazarus, His friends gathered to celebrate at Simon's house. Mary was filled with joy — not only because of the miracle, but because of the way Jesus had rescued her from darkness. Approaching Him, she began to anoint His feet with a flask of pure nard, a very precious perfume (John 12:1-3), and wiped them with her hair.

The perfume filled the air and drew everyone's attention — but instead of admiration, there was contempt. Judas Iscariot claimed Mary was "wasting" an expensive gift that should have been given to the poor (John 12:4,5). John makes clear, however, that Judas' indignation had nothing noble about it: it was greed, since he used to steal from the money the disciples managed.

The Messiah intervened and defended Mary — she had not merely done something beautiful; she seemed to be the only one who had been paying attention to what He had been saying for some time, for she was preparing His body for death and burial (John 12:7,8). Mary did not offer a simple "thank you"; she poured out a striking, fragrant, generous offering.
reflect: Think about the contrast between Mary and Judas/Simon. What helps you keep alive the memory of what Jesus has already done in your life?
Why is a genuine gesture of gratitude sometimes misunderstood by those around us?
How can we truly listen to Jesus, and not just 'pass by' His teachings?

days.title: Total Surrender
days.summary: The week revisits notable figures — Lazarus, Mary, Simon, Judas, Caiaphas — each reacting differently to Jesus' presence, inviting the question: which of these people most represents you?
body: This week, we are revisiting important accounts from the final days of Jesus on Earth. The Bible presents notable figures such as Lazarus, Mary, Martha, Simon, Judas, Caiaphas, and the crowds. Each one reacts differently to Jesus' presence.

What do their attitudes reveal about worship, faith, love, and mission? What practical lessons can we draw from their choices, words, and silences? Looking at your everyday life, which of these people most represents you?

Based on the references below — about Jesus preparing His followers for His death, other accounts of Mary's gesture, and Christ's victory over Satan at the cross — it's time to express what makes sense to you from the word SURRENDER.

days.title: It Is Coming
days.summary: Jesus wept knowing He would raise Lazarus, felt the weight of the cross drawing near as He spoke with Greeks who sought Him, and faced both acclaim and the beginning of the anguish that would culminate in Gethsemane.
body: Throughout the centuries, many have wondered why Jesus wept before Lazarus' tomb (John 11:35). There is one detail we cannot ignore: Jesus knew that miracle would ultimately lead to His own death. In the middle of that remarkable moment, Simon and Judas spoiled it by criticizing Mary — that broke Jesus' heart.

The next day, Jesus was met with the enthusiasm of the crowds, ready to crown Him king (v. 12-15) — and it must have stirred mixed feelings, knowing that many of those shouting "Hosanna" would end up calling for His death before the week was over. Jesus opened His heart when Philip and Andrew brought some Greeks to Him (v. 20-22): He needed to die so that His work would bear fruit (v. 23,24).

Feeling the weight of what lay ahead, Jesus cried out: "My soul is troubled" (v. 27) — anticipating the language of anguish that would appear in Gethsemane. As He surrendered to the Father's will, God spoke to Him and strengthened Him (v. 28); that was the last time Jesus heard the Father's voice, until after the resurrection.
reflect: After this week's study, what became clearer to you about the weight Jesus was already carrying even before Gethsemane?
In what way does this change how you see Him today?
How is Jesus able to balance His own anguish with attention to the Greeks who sought Him?

days.title: The Fragrant Gift
days.summary: Mary did not fully grasp the meaning of her gesture — but the Holy Spirit moved her, and Jesus gave that act an even greater meaning: an early announcement of His own burial.
body: Mary did not fully understand the meaning of her act of love. She could not answer her accusers, nor explain why she had chosen that occasion to anoint Jesus. The Holy Spirit had planned it for her, and she had obeyed His impulses — inspiration does not pause to give a reason.

Christ explained to Mary the meaning of her act, and in doing so gave more than He had received: "In pouring this perfume on My body," He said, "she did it for My burial" (Matt 26:12). As the alabaster jar was broken and filled the whole house with its fragrance, so Christ would die, and His body would be broken — but He would rise from the tomb, and the fragrance of His life would fill the Earth (Eph 5:2).

Mary's act stood in striking contrast to what Judas was about to do. The way Jesus looked at him convinced Judas that the Savior saw through his hypocrisy — and by praising Mary, who had been so harshly criticized, Christ had reproved Judas. The rebuke stirred resentment in his heart, and he decided to take revenge: he went straight to the high priest's palace, offering to betray Jesus.

days.title: When Listening Changes Everything
days.summary: The resurrection of Lazarus seemed to confirm the expectations of crowds and leaders alike — but almost no one was actually listening to Jesus, who was speaking plainly about surrender, self-denial, and the cross.
body: The resurrection of Lazarus marked a decisive turning point in Jesus' ministry. For many, that miracle seemed to confirm every expectation: the Messiah would finally take control. Each group reacted based on what they expected to gain or lose — but almost no one was actually listening to Jesus.

While some wanted to crown Him king and others were plotting His death, Jesus spoke plainly about surrender, self-denial, and the cross. He knew about the religious plans that miracle had set in motion, and even so, He moved forward — His love was greater than the suffering that awaited Him. Jesus used the image of the grain of wheat to teach that true fruit is born when we are willing to let go of control (John 12:24).

Centuries later, a young Christian named Jim Elliot faced a similar dilemma: he gave up everything to bring the gospel to an unreached indigenous people in Ecuador, and a short time later he and other missionaries were killed. To many, it seemed like a total failure — but years later, the gospel reached that tribe, and several people, including some involved in the missionaries' deaths, accepted Christ. What seemed like loss turned into fruit.
reflect: In what areas of your life do you notice your expectations might be speaking louder than Jesus' voice?
In practice, what does it mean to 'listen to Jesus', even when He points toward self-denial or a change of direction?

days.title: What's Going On Here?
days.summary: In the upper room, none of the disciples wanted to take on the humble task of washing the others' feet — until Jesus Himself, the Master, took off His robe and did what no one else was willing to do.
body: For the Passover meal, Jesus and His disciples gathered in the upper room as evening fell. Their feet needed washing, but no servant was present — the task fell to the disciples themselves, which meant someone would have to humble himself. Unfortunately, the mood among them was one of rivalry and resentment, and no one was willing to take on that task.

This prideful attitude broke Jesus' heart. He was about to die and still had so much to share with the disciples, but their hearts were not ready. So He took off His robe, tied a towel around His waist, and, like a servant, began washing the disciples' feet (John 13:1-5).

Peter was scandalized to see the Messiah lower Himself like that (v. 6-8) — he had pictured the Master with a scepter, not a towel. The disciples had prepared the table, but they forgot to prepare their hearts. When Jesus washed their feet, He wanted to show that they too needed cleansing and humility, offering a practical lesson in the very principles He taught.
reflect: Why do you think none of the disciples wanted to wash each other's feet that night?
What did Peter imagine about how the Messiah should act, and why didn't that match what he saw?
In what areas of your life do you resist 'lowering yourself' to serve someone?

days.title: One of You Will Betray Me
days.summary: Judas betrays Him, Peter denies Him, everyone flees — and still, Jesus loved to the end. Christ's love in the upper room did not depend on the response He would receive.
body: The final scenes of Christ's life reveal God's deep and unshakable love for us: "Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end" (John 13:1). Judas betrays Him — and still, Jesus loves him to the end. Peter denies Him — and still, He loves him to the end. All the disciples flee when He needs them most — and still, He loves them to the end.

What happened in the upper room was Christ's love in action. He knew He had more authority than all the kings of the earth combined; even so, He chose to wash the disciples' feet, including Judas'. "God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8).

When Judas was reached by that love, he had to make a decision: would he yield to Jesus' love calling him back, or continue on the path he had already chosen? In the end, Judas hardened his heart against Christ's persistent love and carried out his plans — even though Jesus made it clear that He knew what he would do (John 13:21).

days.title: I Prayed for You
days.summary: Jesus announces that Peter will deny Him three times — but, in that same conversation, He promises to prepare a place for him. Knowing someone completely and still loving him without reservation: that is Jesus.
body: Peter was one of the leading figures among the disciples, but he also had his struggles — he was impulsive and quick to react. We see this in the upper room: when Christ began washing the disciples' feet, Peter reacted right away (John 13:6,7). Jesus said, "If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me" (v. 8), and Peter immediately changed his stance.

Later, Jesus spoke again to Simon Peter: "Satan has asked to sift you like wheat! But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail" (Luke 22:31,32). Peter protested, saying he was willing to die for Jesus — but the Master warned him: before dawn, he would deny Him three times (v. 33,34).

Right after that difficult conversation, Jesus said, "Let not your heart be troubled [...]. I go to prepare a place for you [including Peter]" (John 14:1-3). This precious promise applies to everyone, but in that moment Peter was its immediate target — Jesus knows him completely and, even so, loves him without reservation.
reflect: As you look at Peter's story, what do you come to see more clearly about the constancy of God's love?
Have you ever hidden problems for fear of losing someone's acceptance? How does that compare to the way Jesus treated Peter?
What does it mean to know that Jesus already expected your failure, and still kept loving you?

days.title: Humility That Serves
days.summary: In Auschwitz, Viktor Frankl noticed that those who shared their bread with the weakest found a reason to keep living — a distant echo of what Jesus lived out when He washed feet and offered bread and juice in the upper room.
body: How can someone in the very anteroom of death manage to think of others instead of himself? That question was raised by Viktor Frankl, an Austrian psychiatrist, during his imprisonment in Auschwitz. He noticed that those who shared their last piece of bread with the weakest found a reason to keep living.

This principle finds its highest expression in Jesus. By washing the disciples' feet and offering them bread and juice — symbols of His redeeming grace — Christ revealed that true service is born of sacrificial love. His purpose was not to grant survival, but eternal life.

Humbling Himself to the utmost and taking the form of a servant, He offered grace, purpose, and salvation to His friends. Based on the parallel accounts, the prophecies about betrayal and abandonment, and the meaning of the true Passover, it's time to express what makes sense to you from the word HUMILITY.

days.title: The New Era
days.summary: In the upper room, Christ instituted the symbols of bread and wine, and gave a commandment that, though the oldest of all, was still 'new' because the disciples had hardly ever lived it out in practice.
body: The Passover was, at once, an annual religious festival and a celebration of the deliverance from Egypt (Ex. 12). In the upper room, Christ instituted the symbols of the New Testament — the unleavened bread and wine, representing His broken body and shed blood. The old Passover meal gave way to the Lord's Supper, to help us better understand His sacrifice.

Jesus asks His followers to eat of His body and drink of His blood (Luke 22:19,20) — eating and drinking express receiving something so deeply that it becomes part of us. It is not a mechanical ritual, but something intimate, conscious, and full of meaning. He wants the truth of the gospel to take root in us, and for us to frequently renew our decision to live out that truth.

After Judas left and the supper ended, the Master gave the disciples a new commandment, which, in truth, is the oldest of all: to love one another "just as I have loved you" (John 13:34) — to the point of giving Himself completely. The good news is that Christ never asks anything of us without also giving us the strength to live it out; only He can place that love in us.

Why does Jesus call the command to love 'new,' if it is the oldest of all?

days.title: The Servant Leader
days.summary: Faced with the disciples' proud silence, Jesus Himself rose, took up the towel, and gave an example they would never forget — without arguing, without rebuking, simply serving.
body: On that last night, Jesus had much to say to the disciples. As He looked into their faces, words of warning and comfort were held back on His lips — the disciples felt uneasy, and the glances they exchanged betrayed jealousy and rivalry. The pitcher, the basin, and the towel were ready, but no servant was present, and each one, yielding to wounded pride, chose not to play the part of a servant.

Jesus waited a while to see what they would do. Then He, the divine Master, rose from His place at the table, took a towel, and put it around Himself. With surprised interest, the disciples watched, silently waiting to see what would happen. This action opened their eyes — deep shame and humiliation overcame them.

This is how Christ expressed His love for the disciples: the selfish spirit that motivated them filled Him with sorrow, but He did not enter into an argument about it — instead, He gave them an example they would never forget. "One of the last acts of His life on earth was to dress Himself as a servant and perform a servant's part" (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 518, 519).
reflect: Many leaders would not accept taking on the role of a servant, out of pride or insecurity. What made Jesus different?
Why do you think Peter was so shocked and resisted when Jesus went to wash his feet?
What does the foot washing mean? And why did Jesus ask us to do this for one another?

days.title: The Call to Service
days.summary: Paul doesn't begin by talking about outward behavior, but about something deeper: the mind, the heart, and the inner posture — the same 'mindset' that led Jesus to wash feet.
body: "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 2:5). In this verse, Paul does not begin by addressing outward behavior, but something deeper: the mind, the heart, and the inner posture. The Greek word translated "mind" comes from phroneō, a term that encompasses thought, feeling, and attitude.

What was Jesus' phroneō? The text itself answers: Jesus, "though He existed in the form of God, did not consider equality with God as something to be grasped at any cost. Instead, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6,7). His phroneō was not self-preservation, but self-giving; not the pursuit of status, but service; not domination, but humility.

Jesus taught us that service is not a minor detail of the Christian life; it is central to it. Paul also shows that the path of emptying led to exaltation: God exalted Him supremely. In God's Kingdom, glory is not the fruit of self-promotion, but of faithfulness in service — the cross comes before the crown.
reflect: In practice, what holds us back most from serving — pride, tiredness, or something else?
When you think of 'serving,' what comes to mind first: a burden, an obligation, a purpose, or a privilege? Why?
What kind of service is Jesus calling you to live out today in your family, church, work, and friendships?

days.title: Putting the House in Order
days.summary: Before He dies, Jesus puts everything in order with the disciples in the upper room — He washes their feet and teaches what matters most, because He knows time is running out.
body: In today's culture, when someone dies, the practical responsibilities that follow — funeral, estate, paperwork — end up stealing the space a family would need to simply stop, breathe, and truly grieve. That's why it's ideal that, when someone senses the end is near, they set things in order beforehand: gather the family, say what needs to be said, and reinforce that death isn't a "goodbye," but a "see you soon".

In the final scenes of Jesus' ministry, this becomes clear: before He died, He left the disciples assurances and principles to continue the mission in His absence — He put the house in order before leaving. In John 13 and 14, in the upper room, He washes the disciples' feet to open the way to repentance and renewal. When Judas leaves, Jesus knows little time remains — and there is still much to teach, things they would not fully understand at that moment, but that would prove decisive later .

The teachings of John 14 touch on several themes: Jesus strengthens Peter and reassures the rest of the disciples; He promises they would not be left alone, that they would have the Holy Spirit; He reaffirms the Father's love, promises His peace, and reminds them that the Father longs to be with them.
reflect: If you knew you had little time left with someone you love, what would you make sure to say first?
What "house in order" do you feel you need to set right today — relationships, unspoken words, hurts?
How does the idea that death is a "see you soon" change the way you view a farewell?

days.title: Promises for the Journey
days.summary: Jesus promises to return and reveals that whoever sees Him sees the Father — correcting the idea of a distant, severe God, and assuring us that He hears our prayers.
body: In John 13, Jesus had already given the hard news that one of the disciples was about to betray Him. In John 14, He announces something equally sad: He needed to leave them. The disciples had built memories with Jesus — they traveled, ate, and worked together. It's hard to measure how much they struggled to accept that He was going away.

However, Jesus described His departure as something for their good: He promised to prepare a place in Heaven and return to bring them with Him . When they ask where He was going, He answered: "If you had known Me, you would have known My Father also" , and added: "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father" — correcting the distorted view of a severe Father while the Son would be full of grace. Christ makes it clear that this isn't so: everything He did is exactly what the Father would do.

Twice Christ reassured the disciples that the Father was ready to hear and answer their prayers . Finally, He impressed on their hearts that both He and the Father wanted to dwell with them — an essential truth, because they were about to abandon Him, leaving Him to suffer alone.
reflect: What distorted ideas about the Father have you had, and how do Jesus' words help correct that?
Do you pray believing the Father is ready to listen, or with the feeling that He is distant?

days.title: Help Along the Way
days.summary: Jesus explains that keeping His commandments is the natural fruit of loving Him, and promises the Holy Spirit as a Comforter to help and remind us of what He taught.
body: Jesus declares: "If you love Me, you will keep My commandments" . We could understand this as an order, almost a form of pressure — but that isn't what Jesus is saying. He is describing what love for Him naturally tends to produce. When we love Jesus, keeping His commandments becomes the visible fruit of a personal relationship with Him.

This idea becomes clearer in the next verse: Jesus will ask the Father, and the Father will give another Comforter — the Spirit of truth . Because we love Jesus, He asks the Father to send us the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity, who enables us to love and obey. Father, Son, and Spirit work in harmony to draw us out of sin — and they never set a high standard without first granting, by grace, the power needed to live it out.

Without Jesus' physical presence, the Holy Spirit would continue to guide the disciples and would cause them to remember what He had taught . That promise is encouraging today: the Spirit helps us understand Jesus' teachings and bring them to mind when we need them most.

In what way has the Spirit already "brought to mind" a specific biblical teaching in a moment of need?

days.title: A Guarantee With a Name and a Face
days.summary: Starting from the story of a father who left love notes for his daughter, the text shows that God's promises aren't just words — they have a name and a face: Jesus.
body: The text opens with a true story: after being diagnosed with cancer, a father started writing little notes on napkins for his daughter — simple phrases like "I love you," full of affection. In all, 826 notes: a way of leaving love on record even facing the possibility of not being there.

This story serves as a bridge to Jesus' promises: some theologians claim the Bible contains more than 8,000. The greatest of them stands before us — Jesus will return and take us home. Paul writes that all of God's promises find their "yes" in Him : everything God promised finds its full fulfillment in Jesus. God doesn't guarantee with words, but with a Person.

days.title: Preparing a Place
days.summary: Jesus' promise to prepare a place and return is compared to first-century Jewish betrothal customs — an invitation to wait for His return with joy, not fear.
body: On the last night before He died, Jesus made the disciples the central promise that has sustained God's people throughout the centuries: "I go to prepare a place for you... I will come again and receive you to Myself" . The certainty that Jesus will return transforms the way we face the present, filling us with hope — it was for that desire that He endured suffering and death.

In Scripture, the second coming is often described in the context of a wedding. Jesus referred to Himself as the Bridegroom and told wedding parables to illustrate His return — the wedding feast , the ten virgins . Revelation calls this moment the "marriage supper of the Lamb" .

Seeing the second coming as a wedding greatly changes the way many people tend to understand it. Judgment language has led many to fear Christ's return, but God wants His people to await the great reunion with joy — God's people long for that day with joy , while the wicked face it with dread . Like an engaged couple counting the days to their wedding, whoever treasures this promise doesn't stay silent: they enjoy talking about it, singing about it, dreaming about it.

Do you talk, sing, or dream about Jesus' return, or do you avoid the subject? Why?

days.title: Greater Works
days.summary: Jesus promises that the disciples would do "greater works" — not by their own merit, but through the power of the Holy Spirit working through them after the ascension.
body: "Most assuredly, I say to you," Christ continued, "he who believes in Me, the works that I do he will do also" . The Savior was deeply eager for the disciples to understand the purpose of His divinity being united to humanity: He came to reveal the glory of God, so that humankind could be lifted up by His restoring power. Jesus revealed no qualities that people cannot have through faith in Him — His perfect humanity is what every follower can possess, if surrendered to God as He was.

"Greater works" does not mean a more exalted character than Christ's, but a greater extent — not only miracles, but everything done under the working of the Holy Spirit. Only after the ascension did the disciples fully understand this promise: the scenes of the crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension became living realities, they saw the prophecies literally fulfilled, and they began to search the Scriptures with a faith and assurance previously unknown. As they told what they had experienced, people's hearts were touched, and multitudes believed in Jesus.

Jesus explained that the secret of their success would be asking for strength and grace in His name — until then, they had asked for nothing in that way . He would stand before the Father to intercede for them, presenting the humble suppliant's prayer as His own desire on that person's behalf. Every sincere prayer is heard in Heaven — even if it isn't expressed in clear words, if the heart is in it, it is carried by Jesus to the Father.

days.title: Waiting for the Reunion
days.summary: In the Jewish betrothal custom, the interval between the engagement and the wedding was a time of preparation — just like Jesus' promise to return.
body: In first-century Judaism, the wedding did not take place right after the betrothal. There was an interval between the engagement and the final celebration: during that period, the groom returned to his father's house to prepare the place where he would receive his bride, and only returned to get her once everything was ready.

In light of this custom, when Jesus declares "I go to prepare a place for you" , the disciples did not hear just a beautiful metaphor — they heard the language of engagement, covenant, and reunion. What seemed like a farewell was, in fact, preparation.

The context of John 14 is emotionally intense: Jesus had already spoken about betrayal, denial, and departure. The disciples, confused and unsettled, had left everything to follow Him, and now He was saying He would go away. Even so, instead of ending the night in sorrow, the Master turns that moment into the most comforting of lessons: "Let not your heart be troubled." He does not ignore the pain; rather, He redirects it toward trust.

By promising that He would prepare a place and return for them, Jesus redefines the meaning of separation: it was not a final goodbye, but an interval within a bigger plan. Furthermore, by stating that whoever saw Him saw the Father, He corrects in the disciples' minds the notion of a distant and severe God — and, by promising the Holy Spirit, He guarantees His presence even in His physical absence.

This understanding transforms the way we deal with loss, crisis, and uncertainty. The hope of Christ's return does not eliminate pain, but it keeps pain from having the final word. If the second coming is described as a wedding, the center of the promise is not fear, but reunion.

If Jesus rang your doorbell today, what would need to be put in order in your life, so that you could open the door with joy, without fear, and without reservations?

days.title: The Prince of Preachers
days.summary: Just as Spurgeon used everyday stories to teach spiritual truths, Jesus will use the image of the vine and the branches to explain His relationship with the disciples.
body: One of the most remarkable preachers in the history of Christianity was Charles Spurgeon (1834-1892). For 38 years, he pastored the New Park Street Chapel, in London, becoming known as "the prince of preachers." Spurgeon used to tell the story of a young preacher who worked as a hospital chaplain. After a serious train accident, he volunteered to carry an injured man and, during his recovery, began visiting him often. Spurgeon remarked that the chaplain would always remember that man with deep appreciation, because he felt his weight — when you carry someone in your heart and feel the weight of what they're facing, their name becomes engraved on your soul.

The ability to see spiritual lessons in the ordinary experiences of life is a powerful teaching tool. Jesus, the greatest Teacher of all, did this often: when speaking with fishermen, He used the language of fishing; when surrounded by nature, He drew lessons from what He saw around Him. With mastery, He showed that the natural world reveals God's love.

The Gospels record about 40 parables of Jesus. Interestingly, the Gospel of John doesn't include parables in the strict sense — instead, it highlights metaphors used by Jesus, including longer narratives, like that of the Good Shepherd (John 10:1-16), and shorter illustrations, like that of childbirth (John 16:21). This week, we'll explore one of Christ's most remarkable comparisons: the vine and the branches (John 15).

What spiritual lesson have you drawn from a simple experience in your daily life?
Why do you think Jesus preferred to teach with everyday metaphors, rather than abstract concepts?

days.title: He Lifts Us Up
days.summary: Jesus presents Himself as the true vine — and explains that "cutting off" can also mean "lifting up": God doesn't throw away someone who hasn't yet borne fruit, He cares for them and restores them.
body: John 15 begins with Jesus highlighting the essential connection we need to have: He is the true vine, and we are the branches (John 15:1,5). No branch sustains itself alone; it depends on a source of life that continually nourishes it. The Messiah makes it clear that fruitfulness only happens when there is abiding in Him (v. 3-5).

In verse 2, Jesus says that every branch that doesn't bear fruit, the Father cuts off; and every branch that does bear fruit, He cleans, so it may produce more. The Greek word translated as "cuts off" is airo, which can also mean "to lift up." In a vineyard, this is a common practice: the vinedresser lifts the branches so they receive more light and air, strengthening the plant. In that same verse, the verb translated as "clean" can also be understood as "prune" — Jesus describes two different kinds of care, with the same goal: when a branch isn't bearing fruit, the vinedresser lifts it up — takes it off the ground, recreating the conditions for it to produce; when it's already bearing fruit, he prunes it — removing the excess that drains its energy, so it can produce even more.

With this, Jesus points to two realities that go hand in hand in the Christian life: being accepted by God (justification by faith) and being transformed by Him along the way (sanctification). It's easy to fall for a common lie: that the Lord only accepts those who are "already producing." But God isn't looking for reasons to throw people away — He restores, strengthens, and leads us to grow. In the end, the branches that are removed are those that don't abide in Him (John 15:6).
reflect: Have you ever thought that God would "give up" on you for not "producing enough"? How does this text respond to that?
In Jesus' illustration, what does pruning represent? What has God been asking you to let go of, so you can bear more fruit?
What's the difference between being "accepted" by God and being "transformed" by Him — and why do both matter?

days.title: Enduring Hardship
days.summary: Jesus warns that the world will hate the disciples as it hated Him — but that means they were chosen, not abandoned, and that God is on their side.
body: Knowing what the disciples would face in the years ahead, Jesus spent considerable time encouraging them, as recorded in John 13-17. Often, when trying to encourage someone, we end up "sugarcoating" reality, because it's hard to speak honestly about what lies ahead. Christ, however, knew how to balance both things: He encouraged them, but He was also direct about the challenges that were coming.

In John 15, Jesus explained that the world would hate the disciples — mainly because it hated Him first. But within that warning lies a precious promise: "You are not of the world — on the contrary, I chose you out of it" (John 15:19). God chose us! That changes the weight of the news: Jesus wasn't saying "you're going to suffer because I don't care about you," but "you're going to face hardships because the world hates Me, and I chose you." That completely changes how we face trials — according to our Savior, we face hardships because He chose us, not because He abandoned us.

Jesus went on to explain that the world's hatred isn't directed at Him alone; deep down, it reaches the Father too, who sent Him. He made it clear that Satan is "the prince of this world" and that, as long as we're here, life won't be easy (John 14:30; 15:18,19). The good news is that, if the world isn't for us, God is. Jesus endured the world's cruel hatred because He was secure in the Father's love (John 15:20-23).
reflect: How does the idea of "chosen, not abandoned" change the way you face a current difficulty?
In John 15, Jesus had an encouraging and, at the same time, honest conversation with the disciples. How does that still speak to the church today?
What does it mean, in practice, to be "secure in the Father's love" even when the world opposes you?

days.title: Dependence That Bears Fruit
days.summary: Total dependence on Christ, like a branch depends on the vine, is the central theme — reinforced by lists of references on fruitfulness and on the world's hatred.
body: Jesus presented Himself as the true Vine to show that spiritual life comes only from union with Him. Unlike trees that sustain themselves, the vine depends on support — revealing that, in His humanity, Christ lived in total dependence on the Father (John 5:30), and so we too depend on Him. As branches grafted into the Vine, we receive life, strength, and fruit only through constant communion with Christ; apart from Him, we can do nothing (John 15:5).

Abiding in Jesus means living in continual surrender, faith, and obedience, allowing the Father, as a loving Gardener, to prune and purify us, so that we may bear more fruit. From this union springs a transformed life, in which Christ's character is displayed in us, to the glory of God.

days.title: Abiding in His Love
days.summary: Jesus calls the disciples friends, not servants, and assures them that His love for them is the same size as the Father's love for Him.
body: Jesus assured the disciples: "As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you" (John 15:9). It's hard to imagine a greater statement than that. Jesus invites us to abide in His love, resting in the certainty that we are accepted by Him. When we understand Christ's love for us, it becomes the foundation of our service — whoever serves only out of obligation sooner or later loses heart, but whoever serves in response to His love grows even steadier as the pressure of the world increases.

Jesus gave us the perfect example of this love. He knew He was accepted by the Father and, because of that, was able to bear rejection — the Pharisees' disapproval didn't intimidate Him, because He knew the Father delighted in Him. Christ's love for us doesn't diminish us or treat us with superiority: He didn't speak to the disciples as if they were worthless servants, but related to them as trusted friends, with whom He could be open and sincere (John 15:13-15).

This close friendship with Christ includes constant access to the Father: Jesus invites us to pray according to the Father's will and assures us that He hears and answers (John 15:16). Christ transforms us and restores our sense of worth, because He loves us and receives us as friends. He calls us friends. He was the One who chose us even before we chose Him.

Do you serve God more out of obligation or in response to His love? How can you tell the difference day to day?
What changes when you know Christ calls you a friend, and not a worthless servant?

days.title: Why Persecution Has Decreased
days.summary: A passage from Ellen White explains why persecution seems so rare today: not because the world changed, but because the church has conformed to its standards.
body: Genuine Christianity, if received and obeyed, would spread peace, harmony, and happiness throughout the earth. Jesus' mission was to reconcile human beings with God, and thus with one another. However, much of the world is under the dominion of Satan, Christ's obstinate adversary. The gospel presents principles of life in total disharmony with people's habits and desires — so they rise up in rebellion, hate the purity that condemns their sins, and persecute those who insist on speaking about the just claims of the gospel.

Foreseeing the doubts that would weigh on the disciples' souls in days of trial, the Savior reminded them: "A servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted Me, they will also persecute you" (John 15:20). Jesus suffered for us more than any of His followers could ever suffer at the hands of wicked people; those who are called to endure torture and martyrdom are simply following in the footsteps of the beloved Son of God.

Paul declared that all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Tim 3:12). Why, then, does persecution seem so inactive today? The only reason is that the church has conformed to the world's standards and therefore doesn't provoke opposition — the religion that prevails today isn't as pure and holy as the Christian faith of Christ's day and His apostles. If there were a revival of the faith and power of the early church, the spirit of opposition would revive, rekindling the fires of persecution.
reflect: In the illustration of the vine and the branches, what becomes clear about the importance of staying connected to Jesus?
In everyday life, what does it mean to abide in Christ and in His love through your choices and attitudes?
What strategies do you think Satan uses to draw people away from Christ, and what can you do in practice to avoid falling into those traps?

days.title: More Than Close
days.summary: Just as certain privileges depend on a condition, closeness with God depends on our being reconciled to Him — and He invites us to be called His children.
body: The author shares a personal experience: upon becoming parents, he and his wife discovered something they didn't expect to be so meaningful in the process — preferential parking spots and lines. From pregnancy onward, it was already possible to park closer, use priority lines, among other benefits. It's interesting to notice that these privileges aren't inherent to the person, but are tied to a specific condition — whether pregnancy, having a baby, or another situation that grants that right.

We also know the natural condition of humanity: "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23). This means that, by nature, we tend to live far from God — sin is what creates this separation. This reality can give the impression that there's no hope left: after all, how can we maintain a relationship with a distant God? The greatest danger, however, is getting used to this idea and starting to live as if this distance were normal.

Although sin has separated us from God, He has never forgotten us — there is a plan to reconcile us with Him. The Bible affirms that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting people's sins against them, and entrusting us with the message of reconciliation (2 Cor 5:19). Christ isn't just the way, but also the reward of that way — it's in Him that we find full life. God wants to dwell in our hearts and transform our lives: instead of being merely creatures, He calls us children. Will you accept that invitation?

What does it mean, in practice, to live as a child of God?

days.title: Worth the Wait
days.summary: A personal story shows how the promises in John 16 sustained a couple through years of waiting for marriage and now through a challenging pregnancy — the certainty that the joy on the other side makes every hardship along the way worth it.
body: The promises Jesus made to His disciples in John 16 have strengthened people at different stages of life — including right after graduation and other major life transitions. One person shares his story: he had the conviction that God, in His own time, would give him someone to share life with. Ten years later, he met the person who would become his spouse. Looking back, he can see how the disappointments he went through led to deep inner searching and a genuine commitment to personal healing.

His partner had walked a similar road — frustrations and wounds that led to a serious process of healing. When they met, they realized that both understood what a healthy relationship requires, and were willing to use the right tools to work through the challenges of marriage. Today, the emotional scars of the past no longer take center stage — what remains is the joy of watching God's promises come true.

At the time of this account, his wife is pregnant, but the pregnancy has been challenging — intense nausea, sensitivity to light, discomfort. Even so, the couple chooses to count the blessings they've received, held up by the certainty that when they can finally hold their daughter, everything that weighs on them now will lose its power. Jesus sees the challenges ahead and promises that the joy on the other side is worth the cost of every step.

How do you hold together acknowledging the real pain of a process while also trusting that it has a purpose?
What changes when you know that the joy "on the other side" is part of God's plan, not an accident?

days.title: It Is Better for You
days.summary: Jesus surprises the disciples by saying it is better for them that He go away — because that means the Holy Spirit will come, and His presence today is even more accessible than Jesus' physical company was for the first disciples.
body: Jesus went on telling the disciples that He would soon be leaving (John 16:4,5). Once again, He made it clear that this would be a good thing — but in that moment, they completely disagreed. Imagine being a disciple who spent about three and a half years watching miracles up close and hearing, live, Jesus' most powerful teachings — knowing Him as Teacher, Friend, and Companion. Even the most faithful disciple would have struggled to accept the news that He was leaving.

Christ's statement — "It is better for you that I go away" — challenges Christians today the same way it challenged the disciples. If that promise still holds true, Christians today have more spiritual "advantages" than those first disciples who saw, heard, and touched Jesus — but that only becomes real as we live out the promise, the presence, and the power of the Holy Spirit.

Shortly after the ascension, the first Christians received that power, and the Spirit enabled the New Testament church to carry the gospel to the world (Acts 1:8; 2:1-4). After the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, the number of new converts grew dramatically, far surpassing the crowds reached during Jesus' own earthly ministry (Acts 2:41; 4:4). The Holy Spirit is just as available to us today as He was in the days of the apostles.

days.title: Why Didn't Anyone Warn Me
days.summary: Jesus compares the pain the disciples would face to the pain of childbirth — intense, but purposeful: it points to something full of hope on the other side, and the future joy makes the pain lose its grip on memory.
body: Jesus had been warning the disciples for a while that He was about to leave. Earlier in John 16, He presented this as something good — at first glance, something that might even seem less frightening. However, as He continued this conversation in verses 16 to 24, He made it clear that what lay ahead would be extremely difficult — so difficult that He compared this experience to the pain of childbirth, an intense pain whose full extent no one can truly imagine before living through it.

By using this illustration, Jesus wasn't primarily trying to highlight the suffering the disciples would face, even though that pain was real. He turned to childbirth to teach a profound truth: that pain is not in vain — it points to a purpose and leads to something full of hope and beauty. Just as when a mother holds her child in her arms and looks into his eyes, everything she had to go through loses its weight in the presence of that precious gift.

When our struggles intensify, we can trust that God will bring meaning to what we're going through — He hasn't abandoned us; on the contrary, He is leading us toward a glorious destiny. Jesus told the disciples that they would soon face sorrow, but when they saw Him again, their hearts would be filled with an overflowing joy, impossible to contain — an encouragement that holds true not only for them, but for all of us.

days.title: From Sorrow to Promise
days.summary: Jesus promised that sorrow would not be the disciples' final destination — the Holy Spirit works in the heart, turning mourning into joy, and suffering is never the last word.
body: Jesus promised that sorrow would not be His followers' destination. Although the road includes pain and uncertainty, God is still at work — suffering is not ignored; it's part of a process in which the Lord works in the heart, producing transformation and growth.

This work happens through the action of the Holy Spirit. He dwells in us, guides our choices, strengthens our faith, and sustains us in difficult moments — we don't face our struggles alone or rely only on our own strength. Christ also taught that mourning can be turned into joy: pain is never wasted or forgotten.

days.title: The Father Himself Loves You
days.summary: From the upper room to Gethsemane, Jesus prepared the disciples for the hardest moment ahead — and even knowing they would abandon Him, He assured them the Father's love for them would not change.
body: From the upper room to the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prepared the disciples for the hardest moment ahead and for what would come after. His purpose was clear: "These things I have spoken to you, that you should not be made to stumble" (John 16:1). He encouraged them, warned them about the resistance they would face, and reaffirmed His love for them.

We might imagine that, after such direct and hope-filled guidance, the disciples would never fail or abandon Him — but that's not what happened. It must have been painful to hear that Judas would betray Him and Peter would deny Him (John 13:21,38). Soon after, He announced something even harder — that they would all scatter and leave Him alone (John 16:32).

The Savior was about to be left without human support; only the Father would remain with Him. Even so, His greatest concern was the disciples. He knew they would abandon Him, but His love did not change — so He assured them that, even after they failed, the Father's love would remain steadfast: "the Father Himself loves you" Hours later, when they abandoned Jesus and fled at the very moment He needed them most (Mark 14:50), that promise became the only support they had to hold on to.

days.title: Peace in the Midst of Persecution
days.summary: On the last night before the cross, Jesus did not speak of His own suffering — He wanted to strengthen the disciples' faith, assuring them that, even amid trials, He had already overcome the world.
body: In His final conversation with the disciples, on the night before the crucifixion, the Savior made no reference to the suffering He had already endured and still had to endure, nor to the humiliation He would face. He wanted to give them something that could strengthen their faith, leading them to look toward the reward that awaits the one who overcomes.

"These things I have spoken to you," He declared, "that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world" Christ did not fail nor lose courage, and His disciples were to show that same persistent faith — working as He worked, drawing strength from Him, moving forward by His grace even in the face of seeming impossibilities.

What was the source of strength for those who, in the past, suffered persecution for the love of Christ? It was union with God, with the Holy Spirit, with Christ. Persecution separated many people from earthly friends, but never from the love of Christ — "I will love him," Christ said, "and manifest Myself to him" (John 14:21). When someone faces courts, prison, or even death for the sake of the truth, Christ stands by their side and comforts their heart.

days.title: Joy on the Other Side
days.summary: Jesus promised that the disciples' pain would not be permanent — and the same promise holds true today, for a generation that is emotionally exhausted and pressured by constant comparison.
body: Jesus told the disciples they would face sorrow — and they did. But He also promised that the pain would not be permanent: joy would come on the other side. No one enjoys suffering; we want quick answers and instant happy endings. Even so, John 16 reminds us that there is a kind of pain that makes us grow — Christ compared suffering to childbirth: intense, but full of purpose.

How many times has something that seemed unbearable in the moment later turned out to be a process that made us stronger? It's precisely in these processes that the Holy Spirit is at work — He comforts, convicts, and transforms our perspective. He doesn't remove every crisis, but He walks with us through them.

One of Jesus' most powerful statements is simple: "The Father Himself loves you." The disciples would fail, flee, deny Him — and even so, they were loved. Perhaps our greatest struggle today isn't external, but internal: guilt, comparison, frustration, anxiety about the future. The promise still stands, because God's love doesn't rise and fall with our performance — the peace Jesus promised doesn't depend on the absence of problems, but on His presence.

days.title: Praying for Greater Things
days.summary: A personal account of intercessory prayer opens the week, showing the power of praying for something greater than we ask — a glimpse of what Jesus did in an even deeper way in John 17.
body: A few years ago, a group gathered to intercede for a family, and after weeks of prayer, they saw God move through spiritual revival, reconciliation, and surprising answers. The way a friend prayed, aware of God's presence, gave a glimpse of the power of intercessory prayer.

This lesson became even clearer when they interceded for one of that friend's children, asking for something greater: an encounter that could change his story. On the appointed night, they received confirmation that God had answered — the young man had had a decisive encounter with the Lord at an evangelistic series.

The Gospels record many moments of Jesus, but John reminds us that much more happened than was written (John 21:25). Among these accounts, Jesus' prayer in John 17 stands out, for it reveals a glimpse of Christ's heart and the deep intimacy He shared with the Father.

days.title: Jesus Prays for Himself
days.summary: Jesus begins His prayer by asking for His own glorification — not out of vanity, but so that, through it, the Father would be glorified, and humanity could know eternal life as relationship.
body: Jesus had much to pray about when He finished instructing the disciples (John 13-16) and entered the garden where He would soon be arrested. In John 17, He begins by praying for Himself. He acknowledged that the hour had come, that His time on Earth was ending — and He asked the Father to glorify Him, so that He, in turn, would glorify the Father (John 17:1,2). His greatest concern was that God would be glorified in everything.

His work on Earth was to grant eternal life to those who know God (v. 3). Here, Jesus defines "eternal life" in a surprising way: it is not merely living in Heaven free of problems — though that is true — but Jesus' definition is entirely relational: eternal life is intimately knowing God the Father, and Jesus Christ.

This means we don't need to wait for Heaven to begin experiencing the joy of eternal life — it begins here and now, as we grow in our relationship with Him. Christ knew that His mission of reconciling humanity with God depended on being with the Father again, and He expressed a deep desire to be with Him and enjoy the intimacy the two had shared before the world existed (v. 4,5).

days.title: Jesus Prays for the Disciples
days.summary: Jesus' greatest concern as He prayed was His disciples — He asks for unity among them, protection from the world, and sanctification through the truth, even knowing that Judas had already left.
body: As He prayed, Jesus' greatest concern was His disciples. He pleaded with the Father for "those You gave Me" — a key phrase He repeated five times, with slight variations (John 17:6,9,11,12,24). The continuity of Christ's mission depended on that group, and they were to live "in the world" without being "of the world" (v. 11,14,16).

External threats were not the only risk: there was tension within the group itself — disputes over position, envy, pride. That is why Jesus prayed that, despite their differences, they would draw close and live in unity (v. 11), asking for a deep spiritual union that would reflect the unity between Him and the Father.

Sadly, this prayer would not be answered in Judas' life, for he had already left — but the Savior had not forgotten him. The Messiah's love for His disciples is visible throughout the whole prayer: He revealed the Father's true heart and interceded for unity, protection, and transformation, so that, one day, they could be with Him again.

body: The glorification of God runs through the whole of Jesus' life and is revealed in a special way when He prays for His own. Glorifying the Father is not tied to applause or visibility, but to a life that reflects who God is, even in the midst of surrender and suffering.

In this context, Christ's intercession gains depth. He not only fulfilled His mission, but also cared for those who would go on living in the world. His prayer reveals a heart that protects, sustains, and strengthens, aware of the pressures, falls, and struggles the disciples would face.

Thus, the glory of God and the intercession of Christ meet in the lives of those who remain steadfast — not by their own strength, but because they are transformed and sent to live in a way consistent with the truth. days.summary: Jesus' prayer was not limited to the 12 apostles — He also prayed for all who would believe through them, including you, asking for unity as a testimony to the world.
body: Jesus' prayer for His disciples was not limited to the 12 apostles. He included all of us when He prayed: "My prayer is not for them alone. I pray also for those who will believe in Me through their message" (John 17:20, NIV). Did you know that Jesus prayed for you? Christ's prayers on Earth were only a reflection of the intercession He continues to make in Heaven.

The Savior prayed that we would live in unity — not a superficial union, but a deep bond that exists only when we are united to Him: "that we may be one, just as He and the Father are one" (John 17:21). Unity among us is part of the glory of Christ's character, and God wants to reveal that glory through our lives (John 17:22).

Christ awaits the day when we will finally be glorified with Him. With fervor, He pleads: "Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am" (v. 24). Jesus' greatest longing is for us to be with Him in eternity, seeing Him, and the Father, face to face.

days.title: A Life That Connects
days.summary: Jesus' high priestly prayer reminds us that the Christian faith is not an escape from the world, but a different way of inhabiting it — rooted in truth and sent out in love.
body: "Now this is eternal life: that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). Jesus' high priestly prayer reminds us that the Christian faith is not an escape from the world, but a different way of inhabiting it. We are rooted in truth and sent out in love.

Theologically, it reveals a God who not only acts "for us," but also acts "in us," making His glory visible in restored relationships, transformed character, and a mission lived out in everyday life. Interceding, therefore, is not cheering from a distance, but cooperating with the divine project of forming a people who experience eternal life as real communion with the Father, here and now.

Think of a field hospital set up in the middle of a disaster area: it doesn't remove people from the zone of pain, but brings care to them. Christ's prayer does something similar with us — it doesn't isolate us from the world's pressures, but heals us within so that we can serve without. When the church prays and lives in unity, it becomes that forward outpost of the Kingdom: ordinary people, marked by differences, yet unified by a love greater than themselves.

days.title: Strangely Silent
days.summary: In Gethsemane, Jesus grew ‘strangely silent’ — visibly shaken, unlike the steady, serene Master the disciples knew.
body: There are people who seem unshaken by anything. In Gethsemane, however, Jesus “strangely grew silent” (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 550). The scene was somber — He was no longer as calm and steady as before, but visibly shaken, vulnerable, as if He were breaking down before them.

“As they neared the garden, the disciples noticed the change that had come over their Master. Never before had they seen Him so utterly sad and silent” (same source). The disciples had the privilege of being close to Christ to support Him — but instead, they fell asleep, leaving Christ to struggle alone, deepening His loneliness and His burden.

Christ knew He was entering the “valley of the shadow of death” (Ps 23:4). He understood perfectly that this path would lead Him to death; even so, He did not resist or flee. He summed up the whole experience in the garden with these words: “But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Matt 26:56).

days.title: The Bitter Cup
days.summary: Alone, without support even from His closest friends, Jesus faced the cup of God’s judgment against sin — and still showed compassion for the disciples’ weakness.
body: Jesus took the eleven disciples to the garden of Gethsemane. Near the entrance, He left eight of them and went on further with only Peter, James, and John, hoping they would support Him in prayer during that terrible struggle (Matt 26:36,37). Under the weight of His anguish, He went a little farther, fell with His face to the ground, and prayed: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me!” (v. 39).

Revelation describes divine judgment as the “cup of His wrath” (Rev 14:10). In Gethsemane, Jesus faced the weight of God’s judgment against sin — as our Substitute, He, who had no sin, took upon Himself what we deserved, so that in exchange He might offer us the cup of blessing.

Christ fought this battle without encouragement or help, not even from His closest friends. Even so, in the midst of it He showed compassion: “The weakness of the disciples awakened the sympathy of Jesus [...]. He did not reproach them, but said, ‘Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation’” (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 553). Even in His great agony, He tried to excuse their weakness.

days.title: Put Away the Sword
days.summary: By identifying Himself as ‘I Am,’ Jesus made His captors draw back and fall — but chose not to resist. When Peter reacts with violence, Jesus rebukes him and heals the wounded man.
body: Judas led a group of men to the garden where Jesus was praying. When they arrived, He asked, “Whom are you seeking?” They answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Then He said, “I am He” (John 18:4,5) — in the original Greek, this expression can also be understood as “I Am,” echoing the name by which God introduced Himself to Moses. When they heard this, the men drew back and fell to the ground.

Realizing what was about to happen, Peter struck out with his sword at Malchus, the high priest’s servant, cutting off his ear. Jesus’ reaction was not one of approval, but of rebuke — the Messiah never advocated violence. Jesus said that all who take up the sword will perish by the sword, making it clear that this was never His intention.

Jesus told Peter that He could ask the Father for twelve legions of angels to protect Him, if He wished, but He chose not to — “Shall I not drink the cup which My Father has given Me?” (John 18:11). Afterward, He healed Malchus’ wound (Luke 22:49-51): even in such a tense situation, He thought of others and put them above Himself.

days.title: A Loneliness That Obeys
days.summary: In Gethsemane, Jesus’ suffering was not staged or symbolic — it was real, deep, and lonely, showing that true love bears the weight of sacrifice.
body: On the darkest night of His mission, Christ entered a garden to face a battle that was invisible to the eye, yet weighed upon Him with crushing intensity. There, the suffering did not come from physical wounds, but from the full awareness of what He was about to take upon Himself.

He felt the weight of separation, not because of His own guilt, but because He was carrying what belonged to humanity. His anguish was not staged or symbolic. It was real, deep, and lonely. The abandonment of His friends, the lack of understanding around Him, and the approaching betrayal only deepened the suffering.

Even so, He remained steadfast. His struggle showed that obedience does not eliminate suffering, but gives it meaning. By choosing to stay, even under extreme emotional and spiritual pressure, Jesus showed that true love bears the weight of sacrifice. Based on the parallel accounts of Gethsemane and the intensity of Jesus’ struggle, it’s time to express what makes sense from the word LONELINESS.

days.title: Deeply Sorrowful
days.summary: Jesus’ anguish was so intense that He sweat drops of blood before any physical blow was struck — and, after three prayers, He made the decision: He would save humanity, whatever the cost.
body: The garden of Gethsemane gives us a profound glimpse into the heart of God and the suffering Jesus faced for us. He Himself said, “My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death [...]. Stay here and keep watch with Me” (Matt 26:38). Instead of hearing words of encouragement as at His baptism, Jesus was taking upon Himself what our sins deserve: “The wages of sin is death” (Rom 6:23).

The intensity was so great that He began to sweat drops of blood (Luke 22:44) — before a single blow had been struck, those drops were already falling to the ground. Our sins made Christ bleed before anyone even touched Him. Few scenes show so clearly that sin is not something trivial.

Jesus prayed three times asking that this burden be removed, and each time, you came to His mind — it was for you that He was there. After the third prayer, He “saw the future and made the decision. He would save humanity, whatever the cost to Himself” (The Desire of Ages, p. 555). At that moment, God sent an angel to strengthen Him (Luke 22:43); without that help, Jesus could have died right there in the garden.

days.summary: In His supreme anguish, Jesus went to the disciples longing to hear comforting words — but found them asleep, deepening His loneliness even further.
body: “The loneliness of Christ, separated from the heavenly courts, living the life of humanity, was never fully understood or appreciated by the disciples [...]” (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 448). Satan pressed upon the Redeemer, presenting the situation in the worst possible light: that His own nation had rejected Him, that a disciple would betray Him, that everyone would abandon Him.

“The human heart longs for sympathy in suffering. This longing Christ felt to the very depths of His being [...] He longed to know that they were praying for Him and for themselves” (same source). If only He had known that the disciples understood and valued this, He would have been strengthened.

“Rising up with painful effort, He made His way with faltering footsteps to the place where He had left His friends. But He ‘found them asleep’ (Matt 26:40). Had He found them praying, He would have felt relieved [...] But they did not heed the repeated warning: ‘Watch and pray’” (same source). This discovery deepened His loneliness even further.

days.title: The Garden of Gethsemane
days.summary: The account of Gethsemane reveals a deeply anguished Jesus, bearing the weight of the world’s sin — and, despite the disciples’ abandonment, His love remained steadfast.
body: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on Him, and by His wounds we are healed” (Isa 53:5). The account of Gethsemane reveals a singular moment in Jesus’ life: the One who had always shown serenity and authority now appears deeply anguished.

In the garden, Christ carried a weight the disciples could not comprehend: the weight of the world’s sin. He knew He was entering the “valley of the shadow of death” (Ps 23:4) and that the fulfillment of Scripture required His total surrender; even so, He longed for the company and prayers of His closest friends. His anguish was so intense that He sweat drops of blood (Luke 22:44).

As He was arrested, Jesus showed complete command of the situation — when He declared “I Am” (Ex 3:14), the soldiers drew back and fell to the ground. Even so, He did not resist. In the end, the account reveals Christ’s profound loneliness: while He fought the greatest spiritual battle in history, the disciples slept, and then fled. Even so, His love remained steadfast.
reflect: In Gethsemane, Jesus revealed deep sorrow and asked His friends for support. What does this teach us about the importance of vulnerability?
By choosing to drink the cup of suffering to fulfill the Father’s will, Jesus confronts us: what ‘difficult cups’ come to mind today when we choose to do what is right?
Peter reacted with impulse and violence, but Christ chose surrender and peace. How can we avoid rash actions when defending our faith?

days.title: Condemned Without Guilt
days.summary: Just as Daniel was accused out of envy and his faithfulness to God, Jesus was accused on the basis of lies — and Pilate, even while recognizing His innocence, gave in to the pressure.
body: During the Medo-Persian Empire, Daniel, a former prisoner of war, stood out for his integrity — the Bible records no failures in his life. His faith and faithfulness to God set him apart, and this stirred up envy in his adversaries, who tried to find fault in his work but found nothing (Dan 6:1-3).

They concluded that they could only accuse him if his loyalty to God clashed with the law of the kingdom — so they convinced the king to sign a decree forbidding prayer to any other god. Daniel kept praying three times a day, was reported, and thrown into the lions' den, but the Lord protected him (vv. 4-10, 23).

Jesus was also accused on the basis of lies and brought before an authority who sensed the envy behind the accusations. Although Pilate declared, "I find no fault in this man" (Luke 23:4), the pressure came in the form of a threat — the Jews said he would not be "Caesar's friend" if he did not punish Jesus (John 19:12).

days.summary: Facing false and contradictory witnesses, Jesus remained silent, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy — but when asked directly if He was the Messiah, He declared the truth without hesitation.
body: After Jesus' arrest, the Sanhedrin needed to find "reasonable" charges to condemn Him to death — this was not simple, since He had been careful with His words. The leaders brought in false witnesses, but their testimonies contradicted each other (Matt 26:59,60). In the end, they lined up a distorted accusation about "destroying the sanctuary" — but Jesus was speaking of His own body (John 2:19).

Jesus did not answer most of the leaders' questions. Centuries earlier, Isaiah had already pointed out this silence: "As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth" (Isa 53:7). But when the high priest asked if He was the Messiah, the Son of God, Jesus clearly declared who He was (Matt 26:64) — and was accused of blasphemy.

days.title: Innocent Blood
days.summary: Judas never intended Jesus' death — he was trying to force Him into the role of political Messiah. When he saw the result, he felt remorse, but did not turn to the grace Jesus offered him.
body: The chief priests devised a plan to kill Jesus. Judas, however, did not intend the Master's death — he was stunned to see Him condemned without fighting back. Judas tried to force Jesus to act, to assert Himself and assume the role of political and military Messiah that many expected.

Judas remembered when Jesus refused to be swept up in the excitement of the crowd that wanted to crown Him king (John 6:15) — and now he was trying, once again, to push Christ in that direction. At the trial, however, he discovered that the consequence would be terrible: it would allow Him to be crucified.

Judas threw back the silver coins and left, overcome by guilt and despair (vv. 3-5). He reached that point because he trusted in himself, trying to fit Jesus into his own plans instead of building his life on Him — he never truly submitted to Christ's teachings and principles, and that separated him from the Source of life.

days.title: Faithfulness Under Pressure
days.summary: Jesus' trial exposes more than injustice — it reveals the power of wise silence, the vulnerability of the human heart in the face of fear, and how faithfulness does not depend on circumstances.
body: Before the religious authorities, Jesus faced a sequence of accusations marked by haste, hidden interests, and inconsistent testimonies. The atmosphere was not one of a sincere search for truth, but of confirming a decision already made. In this scenario, His posture draws attention: instead of defending Himself with long arguments, He chose silence at decisive moments.

Meanwhile, outside, fear was shaping attitudes — social pressure led a friend to deny any connection, showing how human frailty emerges when personal safety seems threatened. At the same time, the betrayal that set events in motion revealed how easily interests can override convictions.

This episode exposes the power of wise silence, the vulnerability of the human heart, and the fulfillment of a path already foretold, in which faithfulness does not depend on circumstances, but on the decision to remain steadfast even under injustice. days.title: I Do Not Know Him
days.summary: Three times Peter denied knowing Jesus. When the rooster crowed and their eyes met, Peter saw in Jesus' face not anger, but deep compassion — and that led him to repentance.
body: Peter and John followed at a distance when Jesus was arrested. When they reached the high priest's courtyard, a servant girl asked Peter, "Are you not also one of this Man's disciples?" (John 18:17). Peter denied it — and did so in front of John. They asked again, and Peter denied it again. A relative of Malchus insisted, and for the third time, Peter denied the Savior. Soon after, the rooster crowed.

At that instant, he remembered Jesus' prediction and realized his mistake in having ignored the warning. When he understood what he had done, Peter looked at Jesus, and the Master's eyes met his. Ellen White describes it: "In that gentle countenance he read deep pity and sorrow, but there was no anger there."

Unable to receive grace in that moment, Peter fled and wept bitterly for having denied his Lord and Friend (Matt 26:75). Jesus' reaction shows how He looks at us in our failures — and, as happened with Peter, the goodness of God can lead us to repentance (Rom 2:4).

days.title: Compassion and Forgiveness
days.summary: To hide what he felt, Peter tried to join those mocking Jesus — but when he denied Him with oaths and heard the rooster crow, Jesus' look pierced his heart like an arrow.
body: Peter tried not to show interest in the Master's trial, but his heart was full of pain. To hide what he really felt, he tried to join Jesus' persecutors in their sudden jeering — his manner, however, was not natural. For the second time, he was accused of being a follower of Jesus, and declared with an oath: "I do not know the man" (Matt 26:72).

An hour later, a relative of Malchus insisted, "This one also was with Him, for he too is a Galilean" (Luke 22:59). At this, Peter became enraged and denied the Master with curses and oaths, trying hard to deceive his listeners. While the degrading oaths were still on his lips and the rooster was crowing, the Savior turned and looked directly at the poor disciple.

"To look upon that pale, suffering face, those quivering lips, that expression of love and pitying forgiveness, pierced his heart like an arrow" (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 569,570). His conscience was awakened, and he remembered the promise he had made hours before, that he would go with his Lord to prison and to death.
