days.title: Failing Is Not the End
days.summary: Peter and Judas both fell, both felt guilt — but only one was restored. The difference was not the sin, but the reaction to it: one turned away, the other ran back to God.
body: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" (Ps 51:17). Let's be honest: everyone fails. The big question is not "why did I fall?" but "what do I do after I fall?". Peter denied Jesus three times; Judas betrayed Him. Both felt guilt, but only one was restored.

The difference was not the sin, but the reaction to it. You may have heard of Chuck Colson, an aide to President Nixon in the 1970s, convicted in the Watergate scandal. Before going to prison, he cried in his car and said, "My life is over" — in that moment, he was not repentant, but overcome by remorse.

The difference came afterward, when someone introduced him to Jesus. Colson understood that the Lord was not interested only in the mistake he had made, but in the person he could still become. Remorse drives us away from the Father; repentance makes us run to Him — Colson was genuinely converted and founded a ministry that reached thousands of prisoners around the world.
reflect: When you fail, do you tend to hide from the Lord or to draw near Him? Why?
Is there any guilt you've been carrying for too long that God is already ready to forgive?
In practice, what does it mean to take a step of genuine repentance today, and not just remorse?

days.title: A Troubled Conscience
days.summary: Herod, tormented by his own conscience since the death of John the Baptist, wanted to see a miracle — but Jesus remained silent before him, because He had already said everything He needed to say, through His prophet.
body: When Herod heard about that Rabbi who performed miracles, he began to wonder whether this might be John raised from the dead — his conscience was clearly not at peace. Jesus had been brought before Pilate, and as soon as Pilate learned that He was under Herod's jurisdiction, he took the opportunity to pass the problem along.

When Christ stood before him, Herod tried to strike up a conversation, hoping to see some miracle — but Jesus did not say a word. Herod was offended by the silence, yet he sensed there was something different about this Man. Still haunted by John's death, he was not in a position to give in to the pressure of the Jewish leaders and condemn Jesus to death (Luke 23:8-11).

Jesus remained silent before Herod because He had already said everything He needed to say through His prophet, John the Baptist. This teaches us a fundamental lesson: when Jesus speaks to us through His prophets and His Word, the message must be taken seriously — otherwise, when we meet Him face to face, He may have nothing more to say to us.
reflect: Why did Jesus remain silent before Herod, even when directly questioned?
What does this teach about taking seriously the message God has already given us, before asking for more signs?
Have you ever ignored a clear warning from God while waiting for something more spectacular?

days.title: Condemning an Innocent Man
days.summary: Even while recognizing Jesus' innocence, Pilate offered to exchange Him for Barabbas — and the crowd chose the criminal. Every time we choose our sins over Jesus, we repeat that same decision.
body: The Jewish authorities brought Jesus before Pilate, accusing Him of stirring up rebellion. Pilate asked, "Are You the king of the Jews?" Jesus answered, and Pilate declared to the priests, "I find no basis for a charge against this man" (Luke 23:4). Even so, Christ's enemies became even more determined to secure His condemnation.

Pilate returned to the same question, and Jesus made it clear that His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), adding, "For this I was born [...] to testify to the truth" (v. 37). Pilate answered with the famous question: "What is truth?" (v. 38) — a brief flash of reflection that he did not sustain for long.

Trying to contain the fury of the crowd, Pilate offered to release a prisoner, according to the Passover custom — he asked them to choose between Jesus and Barabbas, a well-known criminal. The people shouted, "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!" (Luke 23:18). Every time we choose our sins over Jesus, deep down we repeat that same decision — "We have no king but Caesar!"
reflect: In what situations do you notice the temptation to 'choose Barabbas' instead of Jesus?
What does Pilate's question, 'What is truth?', reveal about himself?

days.title: The Turning Point
days.summary: A message from Pilate's wife and the insinuation that he would not be 'a friend of Caesar' sealed his decision — even convinced of Jesus' innocence, he chose position over truth.
body: In the midst of the chaotic trial, a messenger interrupted Pilate with a surprising message from his wife — she had seen Jesus in a dream and advised him not to condemn that "righteous man" (Matt 27:19). The turning point came when the crowd cast doubt on Pilate's loyalty to Caesar: they hinted that he could not be "a friend of Caesar" if he released someone who called himself king.

Pilate had to choose: risk his own position to follow his conscience, or preserve his standing by giving in and wounding his own integrity. He asked, "Shall I crucify your king?" (John 19:15) — and the priests answered with frightening irony: "We have no king but Caesar!"

In the end, Pilate gave in to the crowd's demands. Finally, in one last attempt, he washed his hands before the people and said, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matt 27:24). The crowd answered without flinching: "His blood is on us and on our children!" (v. 25) — words that would have tragic consequences decades later.

What does the gesture of 'washing his hands' reveal about trying to escape responsibility?
Have you ever given in to social pressure knowing you were going against your conscience?

days.title: Injustice That Doesn't Silence the Conscience
days.summary: This week's theme reminds us that silencing our conscience for convenience is dangerous — and that Jesus' fall under the weight of the cross reveals that needing help is not weakness, but humanity.
body: This week's theme reminds us that silencing our conscience for convenience is dangerous, that choosing Barabbas instead of Christ is something we still repeat whenever we prefer sin, and that Jesus' fall under the weight of the cross reveals a comforting truth: needing help is not a sign of weakness, but of humanity.

Not even the Savior carried the burden alone. How do this week's passages help us better understand Jesus' trial before Pilate and Herod? By comparing the parallel accounts in the Gospels, an unjust trial in the Old Testament, and Herod's past, we can better understand these final scenes.

With all this in mind, it's time to express what comes to mind from the word INJUSTICE — and to recognize that, even in the face of the worst injustice ever committed, God was in control, turning that moment into the turning point of salvation history.

How can silencing your conscience for convenience happen subtly in your daily life?

days.title: Under the Weight of the Cross
days.summary: Completely exhausted after betrayal, denial, floggings, and abuse, Jesus collapsed under the weight of the cross — and the soldiers called Simon of Cyrene to help Him carry it.
body: Pilate symbolically washed his hands before the people and declared, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matt 27:24). Jesus was handed over to the will of the crowd. By this point, He had neither eaten nor drunk since the Last Supper, and had endured Gethsemane, Judas's betrayal, Peter's denial, the abandonment of the other disciples, and two floggings. Covered in wounds and completely exhausted, He was forced to carry the cross that had been prepared for Barabbas.

He took a few steps and collapsed under the weight of the wooden beams. He rose and lifted the cross once more, but fell again — His human nature could no longer bear it. Realizing He would not go much farther, the soldiers called Simon, from the city of Cyrene, and forced him to carry the cross (Matt 27:32). This moment became a blessing to Simon, and later led to his conversion.

The fact that Jesus collapsed under the burden of the cross shows us that we are not failures when we collapse under the weight of our own cross. He understands. We were not made to carry that burden alone — we need help, help that comes from outside ourselves. Even Jesus needed support to carry the cross.

How does today's lesson help you deal with that?

days.title: The Cost of Rejection
days.summary: By choosing Caesar instead of God as king, the Jewish nation turned away from the theocracy. Pilate, fearing the loss of position and honor, sacrificed an innocent life — and recognized, too late, that Jesus was more than a man.
body: In a voice loud enough to be heard from afar, Pilate asked, "Shall I crucify your King?" But from profane lips came the words: "We have no king but Caesar" (v. 15). By choosing a pagan government in this way, the Jewish nation turned away from the theocracy — they had rejected God as king.

Seeing that he could accomplish nothing, Pilate washed his hands before the people, saying, "I am innocent of the blood of this just man." In that vast sea of upturned faces, only Jesus' face was serene — a soft light seemed to shine around His head. Pilate said to himself, "He is a God!"

"Pilate wished to release Jesus. But he saw that he could not do this and still retain his position and honor. Rather than lose his worldly power, he chose to sacrifice an innocent life. How many, to escape loss or suffering, also sacrifice a principle!" (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, pp. 593, 594).

days.title: The Sound of Silence
days.summary: Jesus' silence throughout most of the trial is an unexpected response to injustice — and Jeremiah reminds us that it is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord.
body: "It is good that one should hope and wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord" (Lam 3:26). Jesus' demeanor draws attention and inspires admiration because of the silence He maintained throughout almost the entire process (Matt 27:14) — an unexpected reaction, since normally, in the face of injustice, our tendency is to rise up and argue energetically.

Jesus stood before the murderer of His cousin, with all the power to destroy him effortlessly and put a swift end to that unjust scene (Matt 26:53,54), but He chose to remain silent. Being right doesn't always require us to voice our opinion.

Trusting that God will intervene at the right moment is a great test of faith, because that intervention may not come when we think it would be best, or it may only be revealed in eternity. Jesus passed the test. And us?
reflect: Is it possible that, like Pilate, we 'wash our hands' in the face of unjust situations around us? Why is rationalizing our 'innocence' dangerous? (Jas 4:17)
Read Amos 5:13. How can we take a stand against injustice and be patient at the same time? Is it worth winning the argument if it means pushing people away?

days.title: An Ignored Warning
days.summary: Jesus explained as clearly as possible what would happen — but James and John came asking for the best seats on the throne, showing just how little they had understood.
body: As they walked toward Jerusalem, Jesus explained to the disciples as clearly as He possibly could what would happen: "The Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests [...]. They will mock Him, spit on Him, flog Him, and kill Him; but after three days He will rise again" (Mark 10:33,34). It couldn't have been made any clearer.

Unfortunately, what happens next shows that the disciples still hadn't understood. James and John came to Jesus with an urgent request about the throne they expected Him to set up: "Grant us that we may sit, one on Your right hand and the other on Your left, in Your glory" (v. 37).

The Master was deeply saddened — He had just revealed the agonizing experience of the approaching crucifixion, and they were more concerned with status and position. The cross should never have come as a surprise to the disciples, but when it happened, they were completely unprepared.
reflect: Why do you think the disciples, even after hearing clear warnings, still asked for status and position?
How easy is it to tune out messages that don't fit the ideas we're already holding on to?
In what areas of your life have you been more concerned with 'position' than with what Jesus is actually saying?

days.title: Mockery at the Foot of the Cross
days.summary: While being mocked by passersby, leaders, soldiers, and even one of the criminals beside Him, Jesus still offered forgiveness to all who contributed to His death, and salvation to the repentant criminal.
body: Jesus' crucifixion took place outside the city, alongside a busy road. Many pilgrims, as they passed by, looked at Jesus with contempt and shouted insults: "Save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!" (Matthew 27:40). The religious leaders also mocked Him, and even one of the criminals beside Him despised Him.

The enemy knew that was the decisive point of the great controversy, so he attacked Jesus' identity with the same line he had used in the wilderness: "If You are the Son of God [...]" (Matthew 27:40; 4:6). But it was precisely because He was the Son of God that He would not come down — He was already, right there, opening the way of salvation.

Most striking of all: in the midst of so much abuse, Jesus still offered forgiveness. He prayed for everyone who was contributing to His death: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34). And to the criminal who recognized his own need and asked to be remembered, Jesus guaranteed access to Heaven — even while dying, He was still saving.
reflect: The people at the foot of the cross mocked Jesus for claiming to be the Son of God. Have you ever been tempted to doubt that God truly sees you as His son or daughter?
Has anyone ever attacked your identity and your sense of worth? How did you react?

days.title: Abandonment, Anguish, and Rejection
days.summary: After three hours of darkness, Jesus cried out the words of Psalm 22 — a cry that seems like defeat, but that, followed to the end of the psalm, ends in confidence and victory.
body: The crowds that had been mocking Him were silenced by a darkness that fell over Calvary at noon. After three hours of intense spiritual suffering, Jesus cried out: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). There may be no worse feeling in the universe than being abandoned.

These same words, written under divine inspiration, were spoken by King David in Psalm 22:1, a beautiful messianic prophecy. Verse 16 reveals that Jesus' hands and feet would be pierced — at a time when crucifixion did not even exist yet as a practice. Verses 7 and 8 anticipate the contempt Jesus would endure, and verse 18 says they would divide His garments and cast lots for His clothing.

That question, which at first glance seems like a cry of defeat, is not the psalm's last word — verse 21 marks a turning point: "You have answered Me." From that point on, the psalm turns into praise and a song of victory.

What does it mean that Jesus quoted a psalm that begins in lament but ends in victory?

days.title: The Cross That Teaches Trust
days.summary: By quoting Psalm 22 — which ends in confidence and victory — Jesus reveals that even while feeling the pain of the separation caused by sin, He still trusted the Father. A pagan centurion recognized the truth that the religious leaders denied.
body: During the three hours Jesus was on the cross, darkness covered the earth, and out of the silence came the cry: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). Although it sounds like defeat, by quoting Psalm 22 — which ends in confidence and victory —, Jesus was revealing that, even while feeling the pain of the separation caused by sin, He still trusted the Father.

His deepest suffering was not physical, but spiritual. Around the cross there was mockery and indifference, but also faith: the Roman centurion declared, "Truly this was the Son of God" (Matthew 27:54). The cross teaches us that our "whys" don't cancel out trust, and that, in the face of Christ's love, we cannot remain indifferent.

How do this week's passages — about suffering in darkness and solitude — help you better understand the hours Jesus spent on the cross? Drawing from the parallel accounts in the Gospels, it's time to express what makes sense to you from the word CROSS.

days.title: How Will We React?
days.summary: Even in the face of the greatest event in history, many react with indifference — but a pagan centurion, a direct participant in the execution, came to the conclusion that Jesus truly was the Son of God.
body: Jesus, the Messiah, the Son of God, bore the cost of the sin of the entire world. This is the greatest and most significant event the world has ever seen and ever will see. Even so, the reaction of many people was, for the most part, indifference. How is that possible?

It's possible to know a great deal about the cross and yet have it make no difference in the heart. Ellen White warned about this danger: "Many who profess to be Christians will take earth's business claims [...] while their hearts are cold [...] in regard to this matter [the cross of Christ], it is a sin to be passive and undemonstrative" (Testimonies for the Church, vol. 2, p. 179).

Thankfully, one of the witnesses changed his mind about Jesus and publicly expressed his new faith. It was someone unexpected: a Roman centurion, a pagan military commander who took part directly in the execution. As he beheld Jesus' suffering on the cross, he reached the clear conclusion that Jesus truly is the Son of God (Matthew 27:54).
reflect: As you read the story of the cross, how does it resonate with you? Or does it feel like 'old news,' rather than something life-changing?
Why is it possible to know a lot about the cross and yet have it not touch the heart?
What does the centurion's reaction — someone unexpected — teach us about who God can reach?

days.title: The Weight of Sin

Now with the terrible weight of guilt He bore, He could not see the Father's reconciling face" (Ellen G. White, The Great Controversy, p. 296, 297).

"Satan tortured the heart of Jesus with cruel temptations. The Saviour could not see through the portals of the tomb [...]. He feared that sin was so offensive to God that Their separation was to be eternal." It was the sense of sin, bringing the Father's wrath upon Him as man's substitute, that made the cup He drank so bitter.

"In that dense darkness, God concealed the last human agony of His Son [...]. Throughout those terrible hours, He had relied upon the evidence given before, that the Father accepted Him. He was acquainted with the character of God [...]. He rested, by faith, on Him whom it had always been His joy to obey [...]. By faith, Christ came out victorious" (same source, p. 605-608).

days.title: The Cross That Changes Everything
days.summary: The cross is not a minor detail of faith — it is the point where everything changes. There, God chose to show His love in the clearest possible way, in the darkest and most unjust place.
body: "But God demonstrates His own love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). If you had lived in Jesus' time, you would probably have felt revulsion at the sight of a cross — because it was known as a cruel, public punishment. Even so, it was exactly there that God chose to show His love in the most definitive way.

On the cross, Jesus didn't just teach about forgiveness — He paid the price of sin. He carried guilt, shame, and condemnation that weren't His. The cross reveals two things at once: how serious sin is, and how much God loves you.

In 2006, at an Amish school in the United States, an armed man attacked children — the case shocked the country. But what shocked people even more was that community's reaction: even in the midst of grief, they chose to forgive. Amish leaders visited the attacker's family, brought them support, and spoke about forgiveness. It wasn't about "forgetting" what happened — it was choosing not to live chained to hatred, because there is a cross on which God forgave imperfect people first.
reflect: What does the cross of Jesus truly mean to you?
Is there someone you need to forgive (or ask forgiveness from)? What's holding you back?
What weight do you need to lay at the foot of the cross today?

days.title: The Torn Veil
days.summary: At the very moment the priest was preparing to sacrifice a lamb in the temple, the true Lamb of God was being crucified — and the temple veil was torn, opening the way into God's presence.
body: Whenever someone brought a sacrifice to the sanctuary, the priest sprinkled blood before the veil, which stood in front of the ark of the covenant. For hundreds of years, this system pointed forward to the ultimate sacrifice of Jesus, the "Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). In A.D. 31, while the priest was preparing to sacrifice a lamb for the evening offering, the true Lamb, without blemish, was being crucified outside the city.

When Jesus breathed His last, the earth shook, the rocks split, and the temple veil was torn from top to bottom — a clear act of God (Matt 27:51). That veil, which had served as a barrier between God's presence and His children, was torn open, making a way for sinners to be forgiven, purified, and restored to God's presence.

The apostle Paul says the veil represented the "flesh" of Christ (Heb 10:20). The tearing of the veil also showed that the earthly sanctuary was no longer necessary, because the price of sin had been paid in full — fulfilling the prophecy: "He shall bring an end to sacrifice and offering" (Dan 9:27, NIV). It was the beginning of a new era.
reflect: What does the tearing of the temple veil mean for the access we have to God today?
Why did the sacrificial system point to Jesus all along?
What changes when we know we no longer need a veil between us and God's presence?

days.title: Personal Conversations
days.summary: Even while nailed to the cross, Jesus had time for two important personal conversations — assuring salvation to a criminal and providing for His own mother's future.
body: When Jesus hung nailed to the cross, no one would have imagined He still had the strength for personal conversations. Yet the Gospels record two significant interactions. One of the criminals crucified beside Him began to realize who Jesus was, and wanted to know if there was still a place for him in the Kingdom — Jesus turned to him and assured him of access to Heaven, even as He was dying.

Later, Mary, the mother of Jesus, was standing there, along with the disciple John. Jesus looked at Mary and said, "Behold your son" (John 19:26); then He said to John, "Behold your mother" (v. 27). From that day on, John took Mary into his home and cared for her — even while suffering intensely, Jesus made sure His mother would be cared for.

It is striking to think that Jesus, suffering under the crushing weight of sin and the pain of crucifixion, was still so attentive to others. As we read in 1 Corinthians 13:5, love "is not self-seeking" (NIV).

days.title: It Is Finished!
days.summary: After hours of agony, Jesus cried out, 'It is finished!' — a death sentence for Satan, and the fulfillment of the plan of redemption God had promised since Eden.
body: At times, Jesus' inner anguish was so intense that it nearly overshadowed His physical pain. Even so, He suffered acute pain during the crucifixion. After hours hanging on the cross, He grew thirsty and cried out, "I thirst!" (John 19:28). In fulfillment of prophecy, the agonizing Savior did not receive even a sip of real water — only vinegar (Ps 69:21).

Finding no relief, Jesus cried out once more: "It is finished!" Then He bowed His head and gave up His spirit (John 19:30). He spent about 33 years revealing who the Father truly is, and finally defeated Satan once and for all — He "condemned sin in the flesh" (Rom 8:3), and Satan's days are now numbered.

"In the Savior's agonized cry upon the cross, 'It is finished,' the death knell of Satan was rung. The great controversy which had been so long in progress was now decided" (Ellen G. White, The Great Controversy, p. 421). Jesus died shortly before sunset on Friday and rested in the tomb throughout the Sabbath, rising very early on the first day of the week.

How does this story change everything for you, personally?

days.title: Conscious Surrender
days.summary: Scripture reveals that Jesus' death was not mere physical exhaustion, but the conscious, voluntary fulfillment of the redemptive plan — a surrender, not a defeat.
body: Scripture reveals that Jesus' death was not mere physical exhaustion, but the fulfillment of the redemptive plan — He died "for our sins," as Isaiah had predicted and Paul reaffirmed. Christ Himself made it clear that no one took His life from Him; He gave it up voluntarily, out of love. Knowing it was a choice transforms our understanding of the cross: it was not defeat, but conscious surrender.

After His death, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, previously discreet about their faith, publicly took a stand for their devotion by providing a worthy burial, while the women honored Him by resting on the Sabbath according to the commandment. So even in the silence of the tomb, we see love, courage, and faithfulness.

How do this week's passages help you understand the true meaning of Jesus' death and burial? Drawing on the texts about "He died for us," "redeemed by His blood," and "bearing our sins," it's time to express what makes sense to you from the word TOMB.

days.title: The Burial of Jesus
days.summary: Jesus died within a few hours — far faster than was normal for crucifixions — because there He carried the weight of our sins, not because the cross 'defeated' Him.
body: Crucifixion did not usually lead to death quickly; victims endured a slow agony, sometimes for days. Jesus, however, died within a few hours (John 19:31-33) — something that surprised Pilate, a man accustomed to ordering crucifixions. He did not die because the cross "defeated" Him, but because there He carried the weight of our sins. Jesus Himself said, "No one takes My life from Me; rather, I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18).

After the Messiah's death, two influential members of the Sanhedrin — Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus — took a courageous initiative to provide a worthy burial. Both feared what their colleagues would think about their interest in Jesus, but that fear did not stop them from doing what God had placed in their hearts. Joseph provided his own tomb.

The Sabbath was approaching, and the burial had not yet been completed. Determined to keep the Sabbath according to the commandment, Jesus' friends had to stop their work and leave it for later (Luke 23:56). They honored Christ in a special way in that moment, understanding that keeping the Sabbath would be an even greater way to honor Him.

days.title: Our Guarantee of Salvation
days.summary: When Jesus surrendered His life and cried out, 'It is finished!', the fulfillment of the plan of redemption was guaranteed — Christ's death proves God's great love and is the guarantee of our salvation.
body: "The kingdom of grace was instituted immediately after the fall of the human race [...]. Yet it was not actually established until the death of Christ. Even after entering His earthly ministry, the Savior [...] could still have refused to be sacrificed at Calvary."

"In Gethsemane the cup of woe trembled in His hand [...]. Had He done this, there could have been no redemption for fallen man. But when the Savior yielded up His life, and with His parting breath cried out, 'It is finished!' (John 19:30), the fulfillment of the plan of redemption was assured in that instant" (Ellen G. White, The Great Controversy, pp. 296, 297).

"Thus the death of Christ — the very event which the disciples had looked upon as the final destruction of their hope — was that which made it forever sure [...] on which centers the future life and eternal happiness of all the faithful" (same source). Christ's death proves God's great love for humanity. It is the guarantee of our salvation.

days.title: Open Access to Hope
days.summary: Christ's death was the turning point of human history — God Himself bears the cost of reconciliation, opening up access to Him based on grace, not merit.
body: "Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place [...] by the blood of Jesus" (Heb 10:19). Christ's death was not merely the end of a life unjustly taken; it was the turning point of human history. Theologically, the cross reveals that the problem of sin is not solved by human effort, but by divine initiative: God Himself bears the cost of reconciliation (2 Cor 5:19).

When Jesus dies, He does not merely forgive — He inaugurates a new kind of access to God, mediated not by merit, but by grace. This changes the logic of religion: we do not climb up to God; He comes down to us.

A simple story illustrates this: a young man tried to "start over" far from everything that reminded him of his mistakes — he changed cities, friends, habits, but he carried the same guilt with him. Until he realized the problem was not the place, but the weight he carried inside. Upon accepting forgiveness and a fresh start, he discovered he did not need to run away; he needed to be reconciled. That is what the cross does: it does not teach us to escape pain, but to walk through it with hope.
reflect: In what areas do you still try to 'earn' access to God, instead of receiving it by grace?
What wounds or guilt have you been carrying that the cross invites you to surrender today?
How would the way you treat people change if you took seriously the access Christ opened for you?

days.title: Doubts and Despair
days.summary: Just as Martha and Mary hesitated in the face of Lazarus's resurrection, the disciples hesitated in the face of Jesus's resurrection — but the One who promised to be 'the resurrection and the life' confirmed that truth.
body: Lazarus's experience should have strengthened the disciples' faith while Christ remained in the tomb. Like Jesus's death, Lazarus's death was "for God's glory" (John 11:4) — and there was also a delay with no apparent explanation (v. 6). When Jesus arrived, four days later, Mary and Martha were deeply shaken, but He comforted them: "I am the resurrection and the life" (v. 25).

After Jesus's death, the disciples went through a trial similar to that of Lazarus's sisters, probably even more painful. Their "Brother," in a very real sense, had also died unexpectedly — and their minds were full of doubts. But the One who had promised to be "the resurrection and the life" confirmed that truth, coming out of the tomb with far more glory than if He had never died.

This parallel teaches us a valuable lesson: there are moments when it's hard to understand what God is doing. Sometimes it seems He allows things that matter deeply to us to "die," as if He didn't care. Yet God knows our pain and our story intimately, and is working in our favor, even when we can't see it.

In what area of your life do you need to trust that God is working, even without seeing it yet?

days.title: Empty Tomb
days.summary: The women found the tomb empty and received the best news in the world from the angels — but when they told the disciples, they were met with disbelief instead of joy.
body: The women were shocked and distressed to find the tomb open and empty. Then two angels appeared and said: "Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen" (Luke 24:5,6). The angels' announcement is the best news there is — a crucifixion without a resurrection would be a death sentence, but the resurrection changes everything.

The angels told the women to go and share this good news with the disciples. You might expect them to receive the message with open arms — but instead, "their words seemed to them like idle tales, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11). Imagine the frustration and pain of these sincere women.

Jesus had already explained: "The Son of Man must suffer many things [...] and on the third day be raised" (Luke 9:22). But they didn't want to hear that message — and when it came true, they still had trouble accepting it. Our preconceived ideas can blind us exactly when we most need light.

days.title: The Greatest Bible Study
days.summary: Risen, Jesus walked with two sorrowful disciples and, instead of a spectacular miracle, offered the greatest Bible study in history — explaining, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, everything the Scriptures said about Him.
body: After rising, Jesus walked alongside two sorrowful disciples on the road to Emmaus. They were talking about the Master's death and the empty tomb, trying to understand what it all meant. Patiently, Jesus corrected them for not believing and not understanding what the prophets had already revealed — and, "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was said in all the Scriptures concerning Himself" (Luke 24:27).

Researchers identify between 300 and 574 Old Testament texts pointing to the Messiah. We don't know how many Jesus mentioned that afternoon, but we can imagine the connections He made — the kind that would make us see the Bible with new eyes. Suddenly they recognized who had been speaking with them, and Jesus vanished. Remembering what they had experienced, they said: "Did not our heart burn within us while He talked with us on the road?" (v. 32).

Jesus touched their hearts not through an impressive miracle, but through a Bible study — strengthening their faith with the same tools we have today. Afterward, He appeared to a larger group of followers, showing that His suffering, death, and resurrection fulfilled the Old Testament Scriptures (v. 44,45).

days.title: Faith That Rises Again
days.summary: On the road to Emmaus, Jesus turned doubt into conviction through the Word — and sent the disciples not to comfort, but to mission, beginning in the most hostile place.
body: On the road to Emmaus, two disciples walked along discouraged, full of doubts and shattered expectations, trying to understand why the One they had trusted had been crucified. Jesus drew near and, instead of performing a spectacular miracle, explained the Scriptures to them, showing that the Messiah's suffering had already been foretold — and as He spoke, their hearts burned, rekindling their faith.

Later, even amid fear and disbelief, the rest of the disciples were also led to believe, not only by seeing the risen Christ, but by understanding, in the light of the Bible, the meaning of what had happened. Then they received a bold mission: to witness beginning in Jerusalem, precisely the most hostile place, learning that God turns doubt into conviction through the Word, and sends us not to comfort, but to mission.

days.title: The Mission Continues
days.summary: Jesus led the disciples outside Jerusalem, ascended before them, and promised He would not leave them to fight alone — He would send power from on high and the Holy Spirit for the mission.
body: It would have been natural for the disciples to flee Jerusalem and never return, after religious leaders unjustly put Christ to death. Even so, Christ said the mission would not begin in Galilee, but in Jerusalem — the city where Jesus was killed would be the city where the announcement of His resurrection needed to begin.

Christ did not choose them for an easy task. The call to repentance would stir up strong opposition; they would not be rewarded with wealth or popularity. Jesus led the disciples out of Jerusalem, and as He spoke His final words of blessing, His feet began to rise from the ground, and He ascended into heaven until He vanished from their sight.

The Messiah's departure, however, did not mean He was leaving them to fight alone. "Now that the Son of man had ascended in triumph, the family in heaven and the family on earth were one" (Ellen G. White, The Desire of Ages, p. 672). Jesus promised they would be "clothed with power from on high" (Luke 24:49), and He promised to send the Holy Spirit to empower them.

days.title: When Hope Seems Buried
days.summary: For the disciples, Jesus's death was the end of a dream — but Jesus, risen, walked alongside them in their confusion, patiently opening the Scriptures, and hope rose again.
body: "Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen" (Luke 24:5,6). For the disciples, Jesus's death was more than a tragedy — it was the end of a dream. They had left everything to follow Him, but now all they saw was a sealed tomb and an empty future.

This experience isn't so different from ours. Sometimes we, too, face moments when something important "dies": a dream, a relationship, a plan, or even our trust in God. During World War II, Corrie ten Boom was imprisoned for helping Jews escape the Nazi regime, lost family members, and faced deep suffering — wrestling with intense doubts: where was God?

Later, Corrie would testify to something powerful: the Lord had not been absent during that dark period. After the resurrection, Jesus didn't first appear at a grand celebration — He walked alongside confused, discouraged people, like the disciples on the road to Emmaus. The resurrection reminds us that God is at work even when we don't feel it, and that death does not have the final word.

days.title: The Loving Savior
days.summary: A near-death experience led Captain William Miller to rethink his beliefs — years later, he would become a preacher who helped pave the way for the fulfillment of Revelation 14.
body: During the War of 1812, Captain William Miller went through an experience in which he came very close to death. It shook him deeply and led him to rethink his deist beliefs. The real turning point came two years later: a powerful sermon deeply moved his community, and Miller was invited to read a sermon in church when the preacher was unable to attend.

Those present noticed how deeply Miller had been touched. That moment marked the beginning of a spiritual transformation that would change his life — and the lives of many others. After studying many of the truths we have seen throughout this quarter, Miller became a preacher of enormous impact, leading many people to accept Christ and teaching the prophecies about the soon return of Jesus.

Miller’s work helped pave the way for the fulfillment of Revelation 14 — a message written almost 1,700 years before his birth. It announces a loving Savior, who will return to gather His people, in fulfillment of prophecy, and it carries a warning: God wants His people to be ready for that return.

days.title: The 144,000
days.summary: The group of the 144,000 receives the seal of God — the name of the Father and the Son on their foreheads, representing a character so firmly established in the truth that it cannot be shaken.
body: Revelation tells us that, in the last days of history, there will be a special people who will receive the seal of God, with the name of the Father and of Christ written on their foreheads (Rev 7:4-8; 14:1). This group is called the 144,000 — Adventist scholars agree that it represents the people of God who will be alive during the final scenes of Earth’s history.

Throughout Scripture, God’s name is tied to His character — when the Lord proclaimed His name to Moses, He described His own character (Ex 34:4-7). So the name of the Father and of Christ on their foreheads represents the loving character of God, showing that this character guides this people’s choices and gives direction to their spiritual life.

The 144,000 are pure before God: “In their mouth was found no guile; they are without fault” (Rev 14:5). To be sealed means to become so firmly established in the truth about who God is — and in His unshakable love for humanity — that faith stands firm, no matter what happens. It was this kind of experience that Christ began forming in His disciples as He gave them His final instructions.

days.title: Preparing for the Crisis
days.summary: Jesus’ final lessons in the upper room (John 13-17) echo powerfully in the three angels’ messages of Revelation 14 — preparing God’s people for history’s final crisis.
body: In the last days of His life, Jesus shared profound lessons with His disciples (John 13-17), aiming to deepen their understanding of the truth. In the time of the end, God’s people need to understand what Christ taught in those crucial moments — Revelation 14 presents several parallels with these essential truths.

The first angel proclaims: “Fear God and give glory to Him, for the hour of His judgment has come” (Rev 14:7). Jesus had already explained that the Holy Spirit would convict the world concerning judgment (John 16:8-11) — and the Holy Spirit will use God’s people, in the time of the end, to bring the world the message of the hour of judgment.

The second angel’s message announces the fall of Babylon, the power that persecuted and oppressed God’s people. Jesus had already warned the disciples about persecuting powers (John 16:2,3). The third angel’s message results in a people who keep “the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus” (Rev 14:12) — echoing Jesus’ repeated invitation, at the last supper, to a deeper faith.

days.title: Faithful to the End
days.summary: Jesus’ final instructions in John 14-16 echo powerfully in the first angel’s message of Revelation 14 — faithfulness in the time of the end is born from a deep relationship with Jesus, exercised today.
body: Jesus’ final instructions in John 14 through 16 echo powerfully in the first angel’s message of Revelation 14: just as Christ spoke of the Spirit’s work in convicting of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment, the angel proclaims God’s judgment and calls for worship of the Creator; both also warn of persecution.

In parallel, they emphasize that loving Christ means keeping His commandments and remaining firm in faith, even when circumstances seem to work against us. These messages show that faithfulness in the time of the end is born from a deep relationship with Jesus, and from a faith exercised today, strengthened by understanding God’s character as revealed on the cross.

This faith not only sustains us in trials, but it drives us to share hope with others. days.title: Faith in Jesus
days.summary: The faith that will sustain God’s people in the final scenes is the same kind of faith that sustained Jesus in Gethsemane — resting in God’s character, even when we don’t feel Him.
body: Despite the chaos that will grip the world at the end of history, Revelation promises that God will have a people who keep “the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus” (Rev 14:12). By remaining faithful to the Lord, this people will face strong opposition and persecution, just as Jesus faced in the final scenes of His life. Those who remain loyal to God to the end will sing the “song of the Lamb” (Rev 15:3).

It’s impossible to build a solid faith overnight. The confidence we will need in the future is born when we exercise faith in God in the big and small decisions of each day. The key to standing firm will be the same kind of faith that sustained Jesus in His moments of trial: “He was acquainted with the character of God [...]. He trusted, by faith, in Him whom He had ever delighted to obey” (The Desire of Ages, p. 608).

The story of the crisis will, to a large extent, be our own story. That’s why we need to ask ourselves: Am I learning to trust the Lord in the challenges I face right now? When I feel alone and unsupported, do I cling to God? Do I remain firm in what I believe, even when my faith is mocked?

days.title: Law and Gospel Together
days.summary: A total and complete trust in Jesus gives the right quality to religious experience — and the third angel’s message requires us to present the law and the gospel together, for they go hand in hand.
body: “The Lord has a work for each one of His loyal people to do, to place faith in Jesus in the position where it belongs: the message of the third angel. The law has its important place, but it is powerless to lend its glory [...] unless the righteousness of Christ is placed beside the law, which ‘is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good’ (Rom 7:12).”

“A total and complete trust in Jesus will give the right quality to religious experience. Apart from this, the experience is nothing [...]. Faith sees Christ as He is: the sinner’s only hope” (Ellen G. White, The Three Angels’ Messages, p. 81).

“If we would have the spirit and power of the third angel’s message, we must present the law and the gospel together, for they go hand in hand.” It was necessary to exalt the great standard of righteousness, but in doing so, many have neglected to preach faith in Jesus — and both are essential for a complete religious experience.

days.title: Reasons to Believe
days.summary: From the origin of the Universe to the existence of a universal moral sense, several reasons point to the existence of God — but Christian faith doesn’t end in logic; it culminates in relationship.
body: “Fear God and give glory to Him, for the hour of His judgment has come. And worship Him who made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the springs of water” (Rev 14:7). The first great reason to believe in God is that the Universe had a beginning — if there was a beginning, there was also a cause. Scripture sums this up: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.”

The second reason lies in the very existence of life — life always proceeds from life, and the complexity of DNA points to an intelligent source. The third involves the human mind, capable of understanding the Universe. The fourth is the presence of a universal moral sense — as Dostoevsky put it: if God does not exist, everything is permitted.

The fifth reason goes beyond the intellectual argument: God’s love can be known and experienced personally. Christian faith doesn’t end in logic; it culminates in relationship. God not only created the Universe, but presents Himself as Father, desiring to dwell in the human heart and reveal Himself intimately. “Taste and see that the Lord is good” (Ps 34:8) is not a theoretical invitation, but an experiential one.
reflect: How do you deal with doubts about God: do they push you away, or can they become a path toward a more mature faith?
How does the idea of God as Creator also change the way you relate to Him as Father?
What does it mean, in practice, to ‘worship the Creator’ in your day-to-day life, beyond worship services and words?
